text:
Krichene and Rendle’s [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) (KDD 2020) shows that sampled ranking metrics can reverse full-catalog model comparisons, even in expectation. With one positive and 99 negatives, HR@10 measures whether the positive reaches the top ten of those 100 candidates; random ranking has expected HR@10=10%. It does not directly estimate full-catalog HR@10 or establish recommendation quality for unseen-item simulator lists. Fixed candidates improve comparability but do not remove sampling bias; retain the pinned evaluator and qualify claims accordingly.

For this design, compare each user’s binary hit outcomes on identical candidates. Per dataset, the HR difference equals (new-only hits − baseline-only hits)/200; one net hit changes HR by 0.5 percentage points and the four-dataset macro-average by 0.125 points. [McNemar’s test](https://itl.nist.gov/div898/software/dataplot/refman1/auxillar/mcnemar.htm) assesses paired binary differences through discordant outcomes. As a practical inference recommendation, bootstrap paired users within each dataset, then recompute the equal-weight macro difference. These intervals concern user sampling under independence assumptions, conditional on fitted models and candidate draws; they exclude training-seed and candidate-resampling variability. Four datasets support conclusions about these categories, with limited evidence for broader domain generalization.

[Cawley and Talbot](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html) and [Dwork et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1506.02629) explain selection bias from repeatedly optimizing noisy validation results. Searching architectures, hyperparameters and epochs on the same 800 users makes the winning validation gain optimistic; ordinary paired confidence intervals do not correct adaptive selection. Record all trials, favor sustained gains over isolated peaks, treat validation comparisons as exploratory, and reserve confirmatory claims for the host’s untouched final evaluation. Fixed seeds ensure repeatability, not robustness across training randomness.
